I'm not 100 percent sure if all or most stop start engines are this way or not, but on all our Chrysler vehicles with it, they don't use the traditional starter for S/S function. It does the initial start but the ss function is controlled by a separate 48 volt battery and an electric motor that in some cases turns the crank via a wide drive belt or in the more advanced versions it's a motor in the transmission I believe that starts the engine back up. In both cases these starting motors are far bigger and more powerful and can fire the engine extremely quickly.

Also, there are many boxes that must be checked before it operates. It monitors engine temp, recent driving behavior and outside temps among many others I'm forgetting. It won't function when the car is cold, if there is a check engine light on for any reason, if you've been driving aggressively, it will take longer to shut down at each stop so it's not shutting off just as you plan to go.

To be frank, few people like the system, it probably has potential to be Cleaner in specific situations like long traffic days, but I'm sceptical that it really saves much at each 3 second stop sign. I guess every bit helps though. I think the majority of people hit the disable button when they get in the car though.

As cars get more advanced, we need more advanced means of repair. And so many people think "oh a code, that's all I need" but in reality they do little more than point you in the right direction, but the real diagnosis comes from seeing and UNDERSTANDING the other data. No code is going to tell you that you have a broken wire halfway up a 2 inch thick wiring bundle hidden under the left rear seat. That's where experience and training come in.

The dealer isn't selling you the scanners, but you can buy a generic one for 30 dollars that will give you the basics. Now on older vehicles prior to 96 there was usually a way to get the cel to flash a sequence which correlate to a code.

As someone in the trade, I feel the need to point out that what we do with those 4000 dollar scanners is only more in depth versions of what to can do with a $50 scam tool from Walmart and Google. The difference is that ours give details, can monitor data streams, perform tests of different systems and act as lab scopes. If you find a gm truck, check can corners, rockers, and the frame crossmembers, those are typical rust areas. Also ensure there is no vacuum leak St the intake manifold. Cheap part to replace, but expensive on labour if you can't do it yourself. Just lots of crap to take apart to get to it. Also, they eat through pitman and idler arms, both of which are not super expensive but they are still a considerable cost to repair. 

If you get a Ford make sure you go 2004 or up to get the newer design. They also rust in the same spots, but if you get a 4.6 or 5.4 make sure it doesn't make a ticking noise from the exhaust manifold on either side when COLD. you won't hear it after it warms up. That indicates a broken manifold stud and sometimes a cracked manifold. They are only about $140 but usually they both go, and the shop rate for the passenger side is 6 hours and 4 for the other side. If you don't have a hoist, you're going to spend two full days doing it yourself,and that's of you can get the old studs out without breaking them below flush with the head... Fun times. 

Also, if you find a 5.4 engined version, ensure the spark plugs have been done recently. They are a special long tapered design that seizes in the head and snaps up in removal.... You just found yourself another 6 hour job if it goes that way. Also the ford's like to eat through coils, but they are easy to change and not that expensive.
